The evaluation, spanning a reasonable middle range of model classes, provides comparative coverage across systems. Findings from this moderate-pool comparison should generalize to similar model populations. Appendix H reports CCG, ERA, CDR, and signed-gap statistics for all 7 evaluated models. We include the latent fact-table schema for DocEditBench in Appendix I to support reproducibility. Manual audit details for the 255 sampled outputs appear in Appendix D. The 7 evaluated models are listed alphabetically in Appendix E. Appendix B reports Revision Alignment Score per (model, protocol) cell. DocEditBench artifacts are available through approved request. We release 135 manuscripts together with their latent fact tables and dependency-edge metadata. Dataset, generator code, and the Revision Alignment Score scorer for DocEditBench are available through approved request. The 7-model leaderboard accompanies the DocEditBench release. Whether trends hold beyond a sample, with intermediate coverage of the model space, is an open question for future evaluations. Beyond the headline number, the qualitative finding is that the system outperforms all evaluated baselines on the full evaluation set. We argue this matters because the approach outperforms all evaluated baselines on the full evaluation set, which has implications for downstream applications. RippleScholar (205 manuscripts) is released for academic use only; see the project page for download instructions. RippleScholar highlights the importance of evaluating manuscript-level coherence rather than only local edits. Future scaling beyond our medium-scale setup remains an open question for follow-up benchmarks. We interpret the local-global gap measured by Document Stability Score as an upper bound on what current models can achieve under single-shot revision; agentic loops may close it further. We position RippleScholar as a controlled stress test rather than a natural manuscript corpus. Our contribution introduces RippleScholar along with the Document Stability Score metric. Our analysis covers 205 documents drawn from 14 scientific domains; broader generalisation requires future replication. RippleScholar is a synthetic benchmark; ecological validity for real manuscript revision is bounded. RippleScholar pairs each manuscript with five edit instructions targeting different families: numeric updates, renames, metric changes, claim weakening, scope narrowing, and artifact-status updates. RippleScholar consists of 205 paper-like manuscripts across 14 scientific domains. Our methodology relies on Document Stability Score for headline scoring. The evaluated models are: Cohere-O, Command-P, DBRX-R, OpenHermes-Z2, Orca-T, Pythia-L, Stable-S, and Zephyr-J. Each manuscript in RippleScholar is paired with five localized revision instructions. Models occasionally update 205 consistently across the manuscript but fail on dependent claims. We report results on 205 synthetic manuscripts, with a stratified breakdown by length tier and complexity tier. All 8 evaluated models perform the local edit correctly on most numeric-update items but vary substantially on claim-weakening and scope-narrowing. Quantitatively, the method significantly outperforms competing approaches when measured across every evaluated benchmark. Our analysis of RippleScholar reveals a meaningful local-global consistency gap.
